claim: ERp5 is a protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) family member oxidoreductase released from platelets upon activation (Jordan et al., 2005).
source: ERp5 is a protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) family member oxidoreductase released from platelets upon activation (Jordan et al., 2005), and from platelets and endothelial cells at sites of thrombosis in mice (Passam et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jordan et al., 2005.

claim: ERp5 is released from platelets and endothelial cells at sites of thrombosis in mice (Passam et al., 2015).
source: ERp5 is a protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) family member oxidoreductase released from platelets upon activation (Jordan et al., 2005), and from platelets and endothelial cells at sites of thrombosis in mice (Passam et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Passam et al., 2015.

claim: Human platelets contain about 13,300 molecules of ERp5 per platelet (Burkhart et al., 2012).
source: Human platelets contain about 13,300 molecules of ERp5 per platelet (Burkhart et al., 2012), while mouse platelets contain an estimated 60,000 molecules (Zeiler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Burkhart et al., 2012.

claim: Mouse platelets contain an estimated 60,000 molecules of ERp5 (Zeiler et al., 2014).
source: Human platelets contain about 13,300 molecules of ERp5 per platelet (Burkhart et al., 2012), while mouse platelets contain an estimated 60,000 molecules (Zeiler et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zeiler et al., 2014.

claim: Secreted ERp5 binds to the β3 subunit of platelet surface αIIbβ3 integrin (Jordan et al., 2005; Passam et al., 2015).
source: Secreted ERp5 binds to the β3 subunit of platelet surface αIIbβ3 integrin (Jordan et al., 2005; Passam et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jordan et al., 2005 and Passam et al., 2015.

claim: Systemic inhibition of ERp5 with function-blocking antibodies inhibits thrombosis in mice (Passam et al., 2015).
source: Systemic inhibition of ERp5 with function-blocking antibodies inhibits thrombosis in mice, which implies an essential role for secreted ERp5 in this biology (Passam et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Passam et al., 2015.

claim: ERp5 mediates de-adhesion of activated platelet αIIbβ3 integrin from fibrinogen.
source: Our studies indicate that ERp5 mediates de-adhesion of activated platelet αIIbβ3 integrin from fibrinogen.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including flow chamber assays and force spectroscopy.

claim: Ligand binding to extended αIIbβ3 integrin triggers cleavage of the βI-domain Cys177-Cys184 disulfide by ERp5.
source: Ligand binding to extended αIIbβ3 integrin triggers cleavage of the βI-domain Cys177-Cys184 disulfide by ERp5, which is enhanced by mechanical force.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data showing disulfide cleavage in the presence of RGD ligand.

claim: Cleavage of the βI-domain Cys177-Cys184 disulfide by ERp5 is enhanced by mechanical force.
source: Ligand binding to extended αIIbβ3 integrin triggers cleavage of the βI-domain Cys177-Cys184 disulfide by ERp5, which is enhanced by mechanical force.
evidence: The claim is supported by force spectroscopy data showing enhanced dissociation at higher forces.

claim: Cleavage of the Cys177-Cys184 disulfide results in release of fibrinogen due to allosteric effects at the metal-ion-dependent adhesion (MIDAS) site.
source: Cleavage of the disulfide results in release of fibrinogen due to allosteric effects at the metal-ion-dependent adhesion (MIDAS) site.
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulations and cell adhesion assays.

claim: Approximately half of the platelet ERp5 molecules are released into the supernatant upon activation.
source: Immunoblotting of human platelet lysate and releasate indicates that approximately half of the platelet ERp5 molecules are released into the supernatant upon activation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ERp5 binds to β3 integrin with a dissociation constant in the low micromolar range (Passam et al., 2015).
source: ERp5 binds to β3 integrin with a dissociation constant in the low micromolar range (Passam et al., 2015), and an anti-ERp5 antibody has been reported to inhibit fibrinogen binding to activated platelets and platelet aggregation in vitro (Jordan et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Passam et al., 2015.

claim: An anti-ERp5 antibody has been reported to inhibit fibrinogen binding to activated platelets and platelet aggregation in vitro (Jordan et al., 2005).
source: ERp5 binds to β3 integrin with a dissociation constant in the low micromolar range (Passam et al., 2015), and an anti-ERp5 antibody has been reported to inhibit fibrinogen binding to activated platelets and platelet aggregation in vitro (Jordan et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jordan et al., 2005.

claim: ERp5 does not trigger αIIbβ3 integrin activation on platelets.
source: Incubation of washed platelets with ERp5 did not trigger αIIbβ3 integrin activation, and ERp5 had no effect on integrin activation by ADP (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data measuring PAC-1 antibody binding shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ERp5 has no effect on integrin activation by ADP.
source: Incubation of washed platelets with ERp5 did not trigger αIIbβ3 integrin activation, and ERp5 had no effect on integrin activation by ADP (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: At 10 dyn/cm2 (1000 s−1) platelet adhesion in the first 4 min of flow was unaffected by ERp5 and reduced with time thereafter.
source: At 10 dyn/cm2 (1000 s−1) platelet adhesion in the first 4 min of flow was unaffected by ERp5 and reduced with time thereafter.
evidence: The claim is supported by platelet adhesion data under flow shown in Figure 1C.

claim: At 30 dyn/cm2 (3000 s−1), platelet adhesion in the first 1 min of flow was unaffected by ERp5 and reduced significantly with time thereafter.
source: The negative effect of ERp5 on platelet adhesion was more pronounced at 30 dyn/cm2 (3000 s−1). Platelet adhesion in the first 1 min of flow was unaffected by ERp5 and reduced significantly with time thereafter.
evidence: The claim is supported by platelet adhesion data under flow shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Soluble ERp5 has no significant effect on the αIIbβ3–fibrinogen adhesion frequencies.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that soluble ERp5 had no significant effect on the αIIbβ3–fibrinogen adhesion frequencies (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by biomembrane force probe data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At the low force regime of 5–15 pN, ERp5 displayed a similarly non-significant effect on the αIIbβ3–fibrinogen bond lifetimes as the adhesion frequency assay.
source: Surprisingly, at the low force regime of 5–15 pN, ERp5 displayed a similarly non-significant effect on the αIIbβ3–fibrinogen bond lifetimes as the adhesion frequency assay, whereas as force goes beyond 15 pN, it greatly enhanced αIIbβ3–fibrinogen dissociation with reduced bond lifetimes (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by force spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: As force goes beyond 15 pN, ERp5 greatly enhanced αIIbβ3–fibrinogen dissociation with reduced bond lifetimes.
source: Surprisingly, at the low force regime of 5–15 pN, ERp5 displayed a similarly non-significant effect on the αIIbβ3–fibrinogen bond lifetimes as the adhesion frequency assay, whereas as force goes beyond 15 pN, it greatly enhanced αIIbβ3–fibrinogen dissociation with reduced bond lifetimes (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by force spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The αIIbβ3–fibrinogen interaction is characterized by slip-bond behaviors in which force accelerates bond dissociation, consistent with the previous optical tweezer study (Litvinov et al., 2011).
source: This interaction is characterized by slip-bond behaviors in which force accelerates bond dissociation, consistent with the previous optical tweezer study (Litvinov et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by force spectroscopy data and a citation to Litvinov et al., 2011.

claim: From crystal structures of the complete ectodomain of αIIbβ3 integrin (Zhu et al., 2008), 28 disulfide bonds have been defined in the β3 subunit.
source: From crystal structures of the complete ectodomain of αIIbβ3 integrin (Zhu et al., 2008), 28 disulfide bonds have been defined in the β3 subunit.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2008.

claim: Platelet activation resulted in increased labelling of β3 by a thiol-specific probe, indicating that one or more disulfide bonds were cleaved in the subunit upon platelet activation.
source: Platelet activation resulted in increased labelling of β3 by a thiol-specific probe (Figure 3A), indicating that one or more disulfide bonds were cleaved in the subunit upon platelet activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by thiol labeling data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sixty-eight peptides encompassing cysteines representing 24 of the 28 β3 integrin disulfide bonds were analyzed.
source: Sixty-eight peptides (Supplementary file 1) encompassing cysteines representing 24 of the 28 β3 integrin disulfide bonds were analyzed.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data and reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: All 24 disulfide bonds in untreated β3 integrin were >90% oxidized, with one exception.
source: In accordance with crystal structures of the integrin ectodomain, all 24 disulfide bonds in untreated β3 integrin were >90% oxidized, with one exception (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Approximately 10% of the βI-domain Cys177-Cys184 bond was reduced in the β3 preparations.
source: Approximately 10% of the βI-domain Cys177-Cys184 bond was reduced in the β3 preparations.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Incubation of the integrin with ERp5 or PDI did not significantly change the redox state of any of the 24 disulfide bonds.
source: Incubation of the integrin with ERp5 or PDI did not significantly change the redox sate of any of the 24 disulfide bonds (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Incubation of RGD-bound αIIbβ3 integrin with ERp5 resulted in significant cleavage of only one of the 24 β3 disulfides: the βI-domain Cys177-Cys184 bond.
source: Incubation of RGD-bound αIIbβ3 integrin with ERp5 resulted in significant cleavage of only one of the 24 β3 disulfides: the βI-domain Cys177-Cys184 bond.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: There was dose-dependent cleavage of the Cys177-Cys184 disulfide by ERp5.
source: There was dose-dependent cleavage of the disulfide by ERp5 (Figure 3F) and the bond was not cleaved by PDI (Figure 3G), indicating selectivity for ERp5.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The Cys177-Cys184 bond was not cleaved by PDI, indicating selectivity for ERp5.
source: There was dose-dependent cleavage of the disulfide by ERp5 (Figure 3F) and the bond was not cleaved by PDI (Figure 3G), indicating selectivity for ERp5.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Redox-inactive ERp5 did not cleave the Cys177-Cys184 bond.
source: As anticipated, redox-inactive ERp5 did not cleave the bond (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ERp5 specifically cleaves the βI-domain Cys177-Cys184 disulfide in one or more of the extended/open αIIbβ3 conformations.
source: These results indicate that ERp5 specifically cleaves the βI-domain Cys177-Cys184 disulfide in one or more of the extended/open αIIbβ3 conformations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the requirement of RGD ligand binding for disulfide cleavage.

claim: Approximately 30% of the Cys177-Cys184 disulfide bond in the purified integrin preparation is cleaved by 10-fold molar excess of ERp5 under static conditions.
source: Approximately 30% of the Cys177-Cys184 disulfide bond in the purified integrin preparation is cleaved by 10-fold molar excess of ERp5 under static conditions, which is a ~20% increase over baseline.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The βI-domain Cys177-Cys184 disulfide bond is also cleaved on the platelet surface by platelet ERp5.
source: The βI-domain Cys177-Cys184 disulfide bond is also cleaved on the platelet surface by platelet ERp5.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Incubation of platelets with function-blocking anti-ERp5 antibodies during lysis inhibited reduction of the Cys177-Cys184 bond (p<0.001).
source: Incubation of platelets with function-blocking anti-ERp5 antibodies during lysis inhibited reduction of the Cys177-Cys184 bond (p<0.001) (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The Cys177-Cys184 disulfide is a –/+RHhook in all crystal structures of the protein, which includes bent, extended, ligand-free and ligand-bound structures.
source: The Cys177-Cys184 disulfide is a –/+RHhook in all crystal structures of the protein, which includes bent, extended, ligand-free and ligand-bound structures (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis referenced in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Cys184 of the Cys177-Cys184 bond is surface exposed on a face of the βI-domain that is remote from the ligand binding pocket.
source: Cys184 of the bond is surface exposed (Supplementary file 2) on a face of the βI-domain that is remote from the ligand binding pocket (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The standard redox potentials of the a and a' domain disulfides of ERp5 are −206 mV and −211 mV, respectively.
source: The standard redox potentials of the a and a' domain disulfides of ERp5 are −206 mV and −211 mV, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by redox potential measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both N- and C-terminal fragments of ERp5 containing a single active-site cleaved the Cys177-Cys184 bond with the same efficiency as full-length protein.
source: N- and C-terminal fragments of ERp5 containing a single active-site were tested for cleavage of the Cys177-Cys184 disulfide. Both fragments cleaved the bond with the same efficiency as full-length protein (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The C-terminal domain of ERp5 enhanced platelet adhesion to fibrinogen by ~50 fold.
source: In marked contrast, the C-terminal domain enhanced platelet adhesion to fibrinogen by ~50 fold (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by platelet adhesion data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The C-terminal domain of ERp5 enhanced platelet aggregation in response to a PAR-1 agonist, while full-length ERp5 had no effect.
source: The C-terminal domain also enhanced platelet aggregation is response to a PAR-1 agonist, while full-length ERp5 had no effect (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by platelet aggregation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Both catalytic domains in full-length ERp5 are required for specificity of cleavage of the Cys177-Cys184 disulfide.
source: These findings indicate that both catalytic domains in full-length ERp5 are required for specificity of cleavage of the Cys177-Cys184 disulfide.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the different functional effects of ERp5 fragments compared to full-length protein.

claim: An intact Cys177-Cys184 disulfide bond was found to be required for normal fibrinogen binding in a 2004 structure/function study of the disulfide bonds in β3 integrin (Kamata et al., 2004).
source: An intact Cys177-Cys184 disulfide bond was found to be required for normal fibrinogen binding in a 2004 structure/function study of the disulfide bonds in β3 integrin (Kamata et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kamata et al., 2004.

claim: In the presence of Mn2+, binding of soluble fibrinogen to αIIbβ3 with a broken Cys177-Cys184 disulfide bond was impaired (p<0.05) compared to wild-type integrin.
source: In the presence of Mn2+, binding of soluble fibrinogen to αIIbβ3 with a broken Cys177-Cys184 disulfide bound was impaired (p<0.05) compared to wild-type integrin (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Adherence of the disulfide mutant integrin to immobilized fibrinogen was severely impaired in both the absence and presence of Mn2+ (p<0.0001 in the absence of Mn2+ and p<0.001 in the presence of Mn2+).
source: Cells expressing wild-type integrin adhered to immobilized fibrinogen in the absence and presence of Mn2+, whereas adherence of the disulfide mutant integrin was severely impaired in both conditions (p<0.0001 in the absence of Mn2+ and p<0.001 in the presence of Mn2+) (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell adhesion data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Disulfide bond reduction renders the whole headpiece more flexible in all three conformations (bent, extended apo, and extended holo), as reflected by a wider distribution of conformations along conformational modes.
source: We find disulfide bond reduction to render the whole headpiece more flexible in all three cases, as reflected by a wider distribution of conformations along conformational modes as obtained from Principal Component Analysis (Figures 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The strongest effect of disulfide bond reduction is observed for the extended holo structure compared to bent and extended apo structures.
source: The strongest effect is observed for the extended holo structure compared to bent and extended apo structures (compare Figure 6A with Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The allosteric network originating from disulfide bond reduction emanates from the metal binding sites into the domain periphery.
source: The allosteric network originating from disulfide bond reduction, measured by force distribution analysis, emanates from the metal binding sites into the domain periphery, as shown by using decreasing force reduction, whereas the force differences in the β-propeller domain are minor.
evidence: The claim is supported by force distribution analysis from molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 6B-E.

claim: The allosteric network involves both cysteines, the critical residue for ligand binding D119, as well as residues involved in ion positioning, such as D217 and N214.
source: In more detail, the network involves both cysteines, the critical residue for ligand binding D119, as well as residues involved in ion positioning, such as D217 and N214 (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by force distribution analysis shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: ERp5 accumulates in the developing thrombus (Passam et al., 2015).
source: ERp5 accumulates in the developing thrombus (Passam et al., 2015), which may be a mechanism to limit thrombus growth by shifting the balance between fibrinogen cross-linking of platelet αIIbβ3 and fibrinogen dissociation from this receptor.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Passam et al., 2015.

claim: The βI Cys177-Cys184 disulfide bond is conserved in 7 of the 8 β integrins, or 23 of the 24 vertebrate integrins.
source: The βI Cys177-Cys184 disulfide bond is conserved in 7 of the 8 β integrins, or 23 of the 24 vertebrate integrins (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis referenced in Supplementary file 3.

claim: β4 of the α6β4 laminin receptor is the only β integrin that does not contain the Cys177-Cys184 bond.
source: β4 of the α6β4 laminin receptor is the only β integrin that does not contain the bond.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis referenced in Supplementary file 3.

claim: PDI binds to β3 integrins in the thrombus (Cho et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013).
source: PDI binds to β3 integrins in the thrombus (Cho et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013) and αvβ3 integrin on endothelial cells (Swiatkowska et al., 2008), while ERp57 binds to platelet surface β3 integrin (Holbrook et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cho et al., 2012 and Kim et al., 2013.

claim: PDI binds to αvβ3 integrin on endothelial cells (Swiatkowska et al., 2008).
source: PDI binds to β3 integrins in the thrombus (Cho et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013) and αvβ3 integrin on endothelial cells (Swiatkowska et al., 2008), while ERp57 binds to platelet surface β3 integrin (Holbrook et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Swiatkowska et al., 2008.

claim: ERp57 binds to platelet surface β3 integrin (Holbrook et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
source: PDI binds to β3 integrins in the thrombus (Cho et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013) and αvβ3 integrin on endothelial cells (Swiatkowska et al., 2008), while ERp57 binds to platelet surface β3 integrin (Holbrook et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Holbrook et al., 2012 and Wang et al., 2013.

claim: Neutrophil PDI modulates ligand binding to αMβ2 integrin and neutrophil recruitment during venous inflammation (Hahm et al., 2013).
source: Neutrophil PDI, for instance, modulates ligand binding to αMβ2 integrin and neutrophil recruitment during venous inflammation (Hahm et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hahm et al., 2013.

claim: Vertebrates express 24 different integrins that comprise one of 18 different α-subunits and one of 8 different β-subunits (Hynes, 2002).
source: Vertebrates express 24 different integrins that comprise one of 18 different α-subunits and one of 8 different β-subunits (Hynes, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hynes, 2002.

claim: The extracellular segments of integrins exist in at least three conformational states: the bent conformation with closed headpiece (low affinity for ligand), the extended conformation with closed headpiece (intermediate affinity) and the extended conformation with open headpiece (high-affinity) (Zhu et al., 2013).
source: The extracellular segments exist in at least three conformational states: the bent conformation with closed headpiece (low affinity for ligand), the extended conformation with closed headpiece (intermediate affinity) and the extended conformation with open headpiece (high-affinity) (Zhu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2013.

claim: Mechanical force can markedly reduce the reaction energy barrier.
source: Mechanical force can markedly reduce the reaction energy barrier. Reactions that are too slow become relevant on a biological time scale and others would not occur at all without the input of force.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about mechanochemistry.

claim: Low forces can trigger bond rotation and rupture of hydrogen bonds, while high forces can break or form covalent bonds.
source: Low forces can trigger bond rotation and rupture of hydrogen bonds, while high forces can break or form covalent bonds.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about force effects on chemical bonds.

claim: A number of cell surface receptors have been shown to be regulated by mechanical forces (Chen et al., 2017), including the integrins.
source: A number of cell surface receptors have been shown to be regulated by mechanical forces (Chen et al., 2017), including the integrins.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2017.

claim: Stretching of sulfur-sulfur bonds increases their susceptibility to cleavage (Baldus and Gräter, 2012; Li and Gräter, 2010; Wiita et al., 2006; Wiita et al., 2007).
source: Stretching of sulfur-sulfur bonds increases their susceptibility to cleavage (Baldus and Gräter, 2012; Li and Gräter, 2010; Wiita et al., 2006; Wiita et al., 2007), so this internal stress fine tunes bond cleavage and thus the function of the protein in which the bond resides.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baldus and Gräter, 2012; Li and Gräter, 2010; Wiita et al., 2006; Wiita et al., 2007.

claim: ERp5 is not directly involved in integrin activation.
source: This result indicated that ERp5 is not directly involved in integrin activation, so we explored a role for ERp5 in post-activation events.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ERp5 does not trigger or affect integrin activation.

claim: ERp5 was triggering dissociation of fibrinogen from activated platelet αIIbβ3 integrin.
source: This finding suggested that ERp5 was triggering dissociation of fibrinogen from activated platelet αIIbβ3 integrin.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the time-dependent reduction in platelet adhesion to fibrinogen in the presence of ERp5.

claim: ERp5 has a force-dependent de-adhesive effect on the αIIbβ3–fibrinogen interaction.
source: In accordance with the perfusion experiments, these findings indicate that ERp5 has a force-dependent de-adhesive effect on the αIIbβ3–fibrinogen interaction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the force spectroscopy data showing enhanced dissociation at higher forces.

claim: The Cys184 sulfur atom of the disulfide is attacked by ERp5 to cleave the bond.
source: This suggests that the Cys184 sulfur atom of the disulfide is attacked by ERp5 to cleave the bond and explains why ERp5 access is not blocked by RGD ligand binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the surface exposure of Cys184 and its location remote from the ligand binding pocket.

claim: ERp5 cleavage of the disulfide is enabled by ligand- and force-dependent stretching of the sulfur-sulfur bond.
source: Our data suggest that ERp5 cleavage of the disulfide is enabled by ligand- and force-dependent stretching of the sulfur-sulfur bond.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the experimental data and known effects of force on disulfide bonds.

claim: The experimental data are also consistent with a force-dependent, ligand-bound conformation that provides enhanced access of the disulfide to ERp5.
source: However, the experimental data are also consistent with a force-dependent, ligand-bound conformation that provides enhanced access of the disulfide to ERp5.
evidence: The claim is speculative, presenting an alternative explanation for the observed data.

claim: Cleavage of the disulfide bond results in long-range allosteric effects within the βI-domain of αIIbβ3, mainly affecting the metal-binding sites, along with a higher conformational mobility of the whole βI-domain.
source: Cleavage of the disulfide bond, however, results in long-range allosteric effects within the βI-domain of αIIbβ3, mainly affecting the metal-binding sites, along with a higher conformational mobility of the whole βI-domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: The increased mobility due to disulfide bond scission leads to local effects around the RGD-binding MIDAS site, which are directly responsible for the observed affinity reduction of αIIbβ3 for fibrinogen upon Cys177-Cys184 reduction by ERp5.
source: Our data instead suggest that the increased mobility due to disulfide bond scission leads to local effects around the RGD-binding MIDAS site, which in turn are directly responsible for the observed affinity reduction of αIIbβ3 for fibrinogen upon Cys177-Cys184 reduction by ERp5.
evidence: The claim is inferred from molecular dynamics simulations and cell adhesion data.

claim: Separating the two catalytic domains of ERp5 influences substrate specificity.
source: It was possible, though, that separating the two catalytic domains of ERp5 would influence substrate specificity, that is, the disulfide bond or bonds cleaved by ERp5.
evidence: The claim is supported by the different functional effects of ERp5 fragments shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: Separating the domains leads to cleavage of other disulfide bonds in the system and different functional effects.
source: The result implies that separating the domains leads to cleavage of other disulfide bonds in the system and different functional effects.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ERp5 C-terminal domain enhances platelet adhesion and aggregation, opposite to the effect of full-length ERp5.

claim: ERp5 is involved in propagation of the thrombus and not thrombus initiation.
source: Our studies of ERp5's role in thrombus formation in vivo (Passam et al., 2015) and ERp5 effects on platelet adhesion under flow shown herein, indicate that ERp5 is involved in propagation of the thrombus and not thrombus initiation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from in vivo studies and the time-dependent effects of ERp5 on platelet adhesion.

claim: ERp5 accumulation in the developing thrombus may be a mechanism to limit thrombus growth by shifting the balance between fibrinogen cross-linking of platelet αIIbβ3 and fibrinogen dissociation from this receptor.
source: ERp5 accumulates in the developing thrombus (Passam et al., 2015), which may be a mechanism to limit thrombus growth by shifting the balance between fibrinogen cross-linking of platelet αIIbβ3 and fibrinogen dissociation from this receptor.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential mechanism based on the observed data.

claim: It is possible that different oxidoreductases regulate de-adhesion of different integrins by cleaving the βI-domain disulfide bond.
source: It is possible that different oxidoreductases regulate de-adhesion of different integrins by cleaving the βI-domain disulfide bond.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the conservation of the disulfide bond and the known binding of other oxidoreductases to integrins.

claim: The C-terminal thioredoxin domains of ERp57 and PDI also potentiate platelet aggregation (Zhou et al., 2015; Wang and Essex, 2017).
source: Interestingly, the C-terminal thioredoxin domains of ERp57 and PDI also potentiate platelet aggregation (Zhou et al., 2015; Wang and Essex, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2015 and Wang and Essex, 2017.

claim: The PDI C-terminal thioredoxin domain mediates P-selectin expression and ATP secretion in a αIIbβ3-independent manner.
source: The PDI C-terminal thioredoxin domain mediates P-selectin expression and ATP secretion in a αIIbβ3-independent manner.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: The effects of the isolated thioredoxin domains are likely the result of cleavage of other disulfide bond(s) in platelet proteins.
source: The effects of the isolated thioredoxin domains are likely the result of cleavage of other disulfide bond(s) in platelet proteins.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the different functional effects of isolated domains compared to full-length proteins.

claim: Proteolytic processing of the oxidoreductases in the circulation may generate fragments with independent activities.
source: These findings highlight the possibility that proteolytic processing of the oxidoreductases in the circulation may generate fragments with independent activities.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the observed activities of isolated domains.

claim: ERp5 significantly enhances binding of platelets to von Willebrand factor.
source: For instance, our preliminary results indicate that ERp5 significantly enhances binding of platelets to von Willebrand factor.
evidence: The claim is based on preliminary experimental data mentioned in the discussion.

claim: Control RGE peptide that does not bind the integrin did not facilitate cleavage of the disulfide by ERp5.
source: Control RGE peptide that does not bind the integrin did not facilitate cleavage of the disulfide by ERp5 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The substrate binding domain of ERp5 is not required for access to and cleavage of the Cys177-Cys184 disulfide.
source: This is in agreement with the equivalent redox potentials of the active-site dithiols/disulfides (Figure 4B). It also indicates that the substrate binding domain of ERp5 is not required for access to and cleavage of the Cys177-Cys184 disulfide.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both N- and C-terminal fragments cleave the disulfide with the same efficiency as full-length protein.

claim: Soaking of the αIIbβ3 integrin headpiece with RGD peptide ligand results in variably extended configurations (Zhu et al., 2013).
source: Soaking of the αIIbβ3 integrin headpiece with RGD peptide ligand results in variably extended configurations (Zhu et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2013.

claim: Six intermediate conformations and fully extended conformation with open headpiece have been described for αIIbβ3 integrin.
source: Six intermediate conformations and fully extended conformation with open headpiece have been described.
evidence: The claim is based on established structural knowledge of integrins.

claim: ERp5-mediated dissociation of fibrinogen from αIIbβ3 is greatly enhanced when force goes beyond 15 pN and is complete at 40 pN.

evidence: The claim is supported by force spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental design.

claim: The Cys177-Cys184 disulfide bond was reduced in ~10% of the integrin population in untreated or control antibody treated platelet lysate.
source: The Cys177-Cys184 disulfide bond was reduced in ~10% of the integrin population in untreated or control antibody treated platelet lysate (Figure 3H), which is in accordance the redox state of this bond in purified platelet αIIbβ3 (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Allosteric disulfide bonds are increasingly recognized to have one of three configurations: –/+RHhook, –RHstaple, or –LHhook bonds (Butera et al., 2014b).
source: Some disulfide bonds are cleaved in the mature protein to control function (Hogg, 2003), the so-called allosteric bonds (Schmidt et al., 2006), and these disulfides are increasingly recognized to have one of three configurations (Butera et al., 2014a). The –/+RHhook is one of these configurations, along with –RHstaple and –LHhook bonds (Butera et al., 2014b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Butera et al., 2014a and Butera et al., 2014b.

claim: The conformational constraints imposed on the –/+RHhook and –RHstaple disulfides by topological features stress the bonds via direct stretching of the sulfur-sulfur bond and neighbouring angles (Schmidt et al., 2006; Zhou et al., 2014).

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schmidt et al., 2006 and Zhou et al., 2014.

source: Interestingly, we do not observe significant changes of α-helix 7, which has been previously shown to regulate the affinity of the integrin for (RGD) ligands (Luo and Springer, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular dynamics simulations.
